title: NOEMIE rejection codes: list, meaning and action
metaDescription: NOEMIE rejection code list: where to find the reliable label, how to classify the cause, fix and follow up on a rejected invoice. The step-by-step method.
contentHtml:
A NOEMIE rejection code is the reason a payer sends back to your software when it refuses to pay all or part of an e-transmitted invoice. It tells you what to fix, provided you read it with its label. Searching the web for a complete list of NOEMIE rejection codes mostly turns up copied tables, with no date or source. The reliable reference is elsewhere: the label displayed by your software, your software vendor's documentation and your local health insurance office (CPAM). This page explains how to read a remittance file, classify the cause, fix it, keep the proof and follow up, without relying on a code found on a forum.

Key points
  • NOEMIE is the exchange standard that lets payers send the payments and rejections for each invoice back to the store's software.
  • A rejection code is never read on its own: the associated label, displayed by your software, is what counts.
  • The official list of codes is distributed to software vendors; your vendor is the first contact for an up-to-date version.
  • Almost all rejections fall into four groups: beneficiary's coverage rights, identification of the professional, invoice content, transmission.
  • Action for today: go through the rejected remittance lines, fix the cause, resend a clean invoice and keep the original remittance file.

What is a NOEMIE rejection code?

A NOEMIE rejection code is a standardized identifier that accompanies a refused invoice in the remittance file sent by the payer. It always comes with a plain-language label and, depending on the case, the number of the invoice and the beneficiary concerned.

NOEMIE (norme ouverte d'échanges entre la maladie et les intervenants extérieurs, an open exchange standard between health insurance and outside parties) refers to the format of the files that the French national health insurance (Assurance Maladie), and some supplementary insurers, send back to health professionals. These files, called NOEMIE remittance files, arrive in your billing software after e-transmission. They report what was paid, what was rejected, and why.

The typical case at the counter: an optical invoice has been e-transmitted, the mandatory insurance (AMO) share or the supplementary insurance (AMC) share does not arrive, and the software shows a rejected line with a code. Another common case: the bank transfer has arrived, but an amount is missing compared with what was expected, because a single line of the invoice was rejected.

The framework for these exchanges comes from the billing and third-party payment (tiers payant: the patient pays nothing upfront, insurers pay the provider directly) rules set by the French Social Security Code. In practice, a rejection is not a final refusal to pay: it is an invoice the payer cannot process as it stands. Once corrected and resent, it can be paid.

To place this remittance file within the whole process, from coverage request to collection, see our guide to third-party payment for opticians.

Where does a NOEMIE rejection appear in your software?

The rejection appears in your billing software's remittance tracking screen, linked to the original invoice. That is where you find the code and its label, not in the bank statement.

The process is always the same. Your software e-transmits the invoice: the FSE (electronic claim form) for the mandatory share, the DRE (demande de remboursement électronique, electronic reimbursement request) for the supplementary share when it goes through that channel. The payer checks it, then sends back a NOEMIE remittance file. Your software imports it and updates the status of each invoice.

Depending on the software, you will see different situations, which should not be confused:

  • Full rejection: no share of the invoice is paid, and one or more codes are displayed.
  • Partial rejection: one line of the invoice is refused, the rest is paid. The amount received is lower than the amount expected.
  • Payment: the invoice is paid, and the remittance file gives the amount and the bank transfer reference.
  • No remittance: no information has come back. This is not a rejection, it is an invoice to track down.

Reconciling these remittance files with the bank transfers into the store's account is a job in itself. It is covered in our article on reconciling NOEMIE files with bank transfers.

Where can you find the list of NOEMIE rejection codes?

The official list of NOEMIE rejection codes is in the standard's technical documentation, distributed to software vendors. For you, the safest source is therefore the label displayed by your software, supplemented if needed by your vendor or your CPAM.

The codes change with new versions of the standard and with billing rules. A list copied onto a third-party site may be outdated, incomplete or specific to another profession. The same code may also not mean quite the same thing depending on the payer that issues it. That is why this page does not reproduce any code: a wrong code would have you fix the wrong field.

The three reliable sources, in order

  1. Your billing software. It displays the label associated with the code on the invoice record or in the remittance screen. This is the reference reading day to day.
  2. Your software vendor. It builds in the standard's documentation and can provide the up-to-date code table, or explain an unclear label.
  3. Your local health insurance office (CPAM). For the mandatory share, it can clarify the reason for a rejection that still makes no sense.

For the supplementary share, when the invoice goes through a third-party payment platform, the reason is often also visible in the platform's professional portal. Our page on third-party payment portals lists where to look for each operator.

The trap: making a correction based on a code read on a forum, without looking at the label of your own remittance file. Two sources can give two different meanings. Only the label you received says what the payer objects to in this invoice.

Why is an invoice rejected?

There are four groups of causes: the beneficiary's coverage rights, the identification of the professional or the prescriber, the invoice content, and the transmission itself. The code's label almost always tells you which group you are dealing with.

Classify first, then fix: this is the safest method. It keeps you from changing three fields at random and resending an invoice that will be rejected a second time.

Group of causesWhat the label says, in essenceWhere to checkFix
Beneficiary's coverage rightsUnknown insured person or beneficiary, closed coverage rights, insurer or contract not recognizedCarte Vitale, certificate of coverage rights, the customer's third-party payment cardUpdate the identity, the beneficiary rank, the insurer or the coverage dates, then resend
IdentificationProfessional, prescriber or identification number not recognizedStore settings in the software, prescriptionCorrect the prescriber's or the store's identifier, check the settings
Invoice contentProduct code, quantity, amount, date or consistency with the prescriptionInvoice lines, LPP codes, standardized quoteCorrect the line at fault, without touching the lines already paid
TransmissionDuplicate, invoice already received, unreadable format or batchSubmission history, e-transmission logCheck whether the invoice has already been paid before resending; otherwise, contact the software vendor

The LPP (list of reimbursable products and services) is the nomenclature that sets the codes for lenses, frames and services. An LPP code inconsistent with the eyewear or the class (A for the 100% Santé (zero out-of-pocket scheme) basket, B for free pricing) is one of the causes in the “invoice content” group.

Duplicates deserve special attention. Resending an invoice that has already been paid creates a new rejection, and sometimes an overpayment to be repaid later. Before any resubmission, check in the software that no payment has been received for the same invoice.

Many of these causes can be prevented before sending. Our article on how to reduce CPAM rejections without changing software details the checks to put in place upstream.

What should you do based on the code received?

Read the label, classify the cause into one of the four groups, correct only the data at fault, then resend a clean invoice. Do not recreate an entire file when only one line is rejected.

  1. Open the remittance file in the software. Find the invoice, the beneficiary, the code and its label. Note the date of the remittance file.
  2. Identify the share concerned. Mandatory share, supplementary share, or both: the contact will not be the same.
  3. Classify the cause. Coverage rights, identification, content or transmission. If you are unsure about the label, ask your vendor what it means before changing anything.
  4. Check that no payment has already arrived. Check the invoice history and the bank reconciliation to avoid a duplicate.
  5. Correct the data at fault. Identity, beneficiary rank, insurer, LPP code, prescriber identifier: a targeted, documented correction.
  6. Resend the corrected invoice. Use your software's rebilling or resubmission function, following the procedure set by your vendor.
  7. Watch the next remittance file. Note the resubmission date and check that the next NOEMIE remittance file does report a payment.

When the cause relates to the customer's coverage rights, the correction often requires a document to request: an up-to-date certificate, a new third-party payment card. Let the customer know as early as possible, without handing them the work of correcting it.

When these rejections pile up across several platforms and several stores, the daily review becomes a job in its own right. This is the work Granit's agents take over: they track the remittance files, spot rejected invoices or those left unanswered, and flag to the team what needs a correction.

What proof should you keep after a NOEMIE rejection?

Keep the original NOEMIE remittance file, the original invoice, the corrected invoice and the document that justifies the correction. These four items are enough to rebuild the file if the payer disputes it or if an audit takes place.

  • The original remittance file with the code, the label and the date, as displayed in the software.
  • The original invoice, without deleting it, even after correction.
  • The resent invoice, with its e-transmission date.
  • The supporting document: certificate of coverage rights, prescription, standardized quote, third-party payment card.
  • The exchanges with the CPAM, the platform or the vendor: date, contact, answer received.

These documents contain personal data and health data. Their retention is governed by the European General Data Protection Regulation: access limited to the people who handle the file, storage in the software or a secure space, never in a personal mailbox.

The right habit: add a note to the invoice record for every action (“corrected beneficiary rank, resent on …”). The day a colleague picks up the file, they know where the invoice stands without rereading everything.

How long should you wait before following up after a rejection?

There is no single deadline: each payer has its own pace for processing and sending back remittance files. Good practice is to set an internal review schedule and to follow up as soon as a resent invoice stays without a remittance file beyond what you usually see for that payer.

In practice, most stores organize themselves around two routines. A regular review of remittance files, to handle rejections while the file is still fresh. And a review of older invoices, to spot those that have received neither payment nor rejection.

An invoice with no remittance at all is not an invoice in progress: it is an invoice that may never have been received. It is handled as a transmission anomaly, not as a rejection. First check your software's e-transmission log.

Do not let rejections age. The older a file is, the harder it is to get a document from the customer or an explanation from the payer. The applicable billing deadlines come from the French Social Security Code and the agreements with the health insurance system: if you are unsure about an old file, ask your CPAM before resending it.

When should you escalate a NOEMIE rejection, and to whom?

Escalate when the label still makes no sense, when the same invoice is rejected twice with the same reason, or when the reason does not match the file. The right contact depends on the share rejected and the cause.

SituationWho to contactWhat to provide
Mandatory share rejected, reason unclear or disputedYour CPAM, through the channels reserved for health professionalsInvoice number, date, code and label, correction already attempted
Supplementary share rejected through a platformThe professional services team of the platform concernedCoverage approval reference, invoice number, reason displayed
Format rejection, unreadable batch, unexplained duplicateYour software vendorE-transmission log, batch date, remittance file received
Missing label or code unknown to the softwareYour software vendorScreenshot of the remittance file, software version

For supplementary shares, the contact details and professional portals of the main operators are gathered on our platform pages, for example those for Viamedis and Almerys.

Before calling, prepare the complete file. An effective escalation fits in one sentence: which invoice, which reason, which correction has already been made, and what you expect from the person you are contacting. That is what makes the difference between a useful call and a ticket that goes around in circles.

Keep the exact label displayed in the remittance file: it, and not a code copied from elsewhere, tells you what to fix.

faqItems.question: What is a NOEMIE rejection code?
faqItems.answer: A NOEMIE rejection code is the standardized reason a payer sends back to the store's software when it refuses to pay all or part of an e-transmitted invoice. It always comes with a plain-language label. It is not a final refusal: once corrected and resent, the invoice can be paid.

faqItems.question: Where can I find the list of NOEMIE rejection codes?
faqItems.answer: The official list is in the technical documentation of the NOEMIE standard, distributed to software vendors. Day to day, the reliable source is the label your billing software displays next to the code. For an up-to-date table or an unclear label, ask your software vendor, then your local health insurance office (CPAM) for the mandatory share.

faqItems.question: What should I do based on the NOEMIE rejection code received?
faqItems.answer: Read the label, then classify the cause: beneficiary's coverage rights, identification of the professional or the prescriber, invoice content, or transmission. Check that no payment has already arrived, correct only the data at fault and resend the invoice. Then watch the next remittance file to confirm payment.

faqItems.question: Do I have to redo the whole invoice after a NOEMIE rejection?
faqItems.answer: No, correct only the data at fault and resend the invoice using the function your software provides. When only one line is rejected, the lines already paid must not be resent, or you will create a duplicate. Keep the original invoice and the original remittance file as proof.

faqItems.question: Who should I contact when a NOEMIE rejection still makes no sense?
faqItems.answer: For a rejection of the mandatory share, contact your local health insurance office (CPAM) through the channels reserved for health professionals. For the supplementary share, contact the professional services team of the platform concerned. For a format issue, a batch issue or a code your software does not recognize, your software vendor is the right contact.
